ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Corpus Christi, Texas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Corpus Christi, Texas: wall-thickness surveys on corroded piping, vessels and tanks, and angle-beam examination of welds in refinery, terminal, LNG and fabrication work around the ship channel. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope and work to your written practice and the governing code. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Request a UT quote for Corpus Christi and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Corpus Christi

Corpus Christi is built around the Port of Corpus Christi, which describes itself as the nation's largest energy export gateway and keeps a 54-foot channel open for crude, refined products and bulk cargo. That single fact shapes almost every UT job in the area. Refineries on the Inner Harbor run process piping, heat exchangers, columns and storage that corrode from the inside, and the coastal atmosphere attacks them from the outside. Terminals along the channel carry large aboveground tanks, loading arms, dock piping and pipe racks. LNG liquefaction and export facilities on the La Quinta side add cryogenic and high-pressure piping with strict weld requirements.

Away from the water, the same inspection questions repeat in a different form. Steel and pipe products move through the port, wind-energy project cargo needs lifting gear and heavy structural welds, and the new Harbor Bridge replacement carries a cable-stayed steel and concrete superstructure across the channel. Ultrasonic testing is the method that answers the question these assets share: how much sound wall is left, and are the welds free of planar flaws that a surface method cannot see?

What UT finds in Coastal Bend steel, and what it misses

A sound pulse travels through the metal at a known velocity and reflects from the back wall or from any interface in between. Measuring the time gives thickness; reading the amplitude and position of an echo that arrives early reveals a discontinuity. In carbon steel piping and plate, which dominate the Coastal Bend, the method sees lack of fusion, cracks, slag lines and laminations that never break the surface, so it complements magnetic particle and penetrant inspection rather than replacing them.

UT has limits that matter here. Pitting under insulation can scatter the sound and give a noisy reading, so the technician scans around the spot instead of trusting one number. Heavy scale, flaking paint and rough weld caps prevent the probe from coupling. Coarse-grained castings and austenitic stainless welds attenuate the beam, which can require a different probe or a different method. Very thin wall below the practical range of the probe cannot be measured with a standard dual-element transducer. A good report says what was and was not examined.

Thickness surveys on piping, vessels and tanks

Most ultrasonic work on corroding plant equipment is thickness measurement at condition monitoring locations. On a Corpus Christi refinery or terminal that means a grid of marked points on elbows, tees, injection points, dead legs, tank shell courses and vessel heads, read on every inspection cycle so the corrosion rate can be calculated. Our technicians use dual-element probes, which handle corroded and pitted surfaces better than single-element probes, and calibrate on a step block of the same material before each set of readings. ASTM E797 and the thickness provisions of ASME Section V Article 5 and Article 23 describe the practice.

The data goes to the person who decides remaining life. Under API 510, API 570 and API 653 the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection, and Atlantis supplies the thickness readings, the grid sketches and the comparison to previous values. We do not act as the inspector of record. For tanks, the same approach applies to shell courses and annular plates when the owner needs a quick picture of wall loss before a planned outage, though floor mapping is a separate scope we do not include here.

Weld examination with angle beams

For groove welds in pressure piping, vessels and structural steel, the technician uses an angle-beam shear-wave probe, usually 45, 60 or 70 degrees, and a reference level built from side-drilled holes in a calibration block of the same material and thickness. The probe is moved across the weld and heat-affected zone from both sides where access allows, because a flaw that is invisible from one face may be obvious from the other. Indications are evaluated against the acceptance table the code names.

The code decides how much of this work exists. ASME B31.3 includes provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, API 1104 covers pipeline girth welds, and AWS D1.1 sets its own ultrasonic acceptance rules for groove welds in structural steel. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 describes ultrasonic examination of welds in pressure vessels. When an owner or fabricator wants UT to take the place of radiography on a weld, the substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector before work begins. We write the procedure to the code edition in the contract, not the one we happen to prefer.

Codes and the Texas regulatory picture

Corpus Christi work sits inside several overlapping rules. The Texas Boiler Law, Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code, is administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, which registers boilers and which relies on Authorized Inspectors from inspection agencies and on state deputy inspectors for inspections. Process units fall under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j), which requires inspection and testing of process equipment to recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice. The Railroad Commission of Texas oversees intrastate pipeline safety under 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, and interstate lines come under PHMSA. State highway bridges are normally fabricated and inspected under AWS D1.5.

Which document governs a given UT job depends on the asset, so the first conversation is always about the contract: the code, the edition, the acceptance criteria and who signs. The related Texas inspection page collects how we handle the state's work, and the national ultrasonic testing service page describes what you receive on any UT job.

Who does the work and what the report contains

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the results. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the reports; Anoop Rayavarapu, the founder, holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT and stands behind the procedures. If you want your own written practice used, we work to it. If you need one built or reviewed, see written practice development and Level III consulting.

A UT report from us identifies each component, the procedure and its revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the couplant and the surface condition, the technician and qualification level, and the date. Thickness work lists every reading against the nominal and previous value with a sketch of the grid. Weld work lists each recordable indication by location, length and amplitude and states accept or reject against the named criteria. Nothing is rounded to look better than it is.

From readings to decisions: corrosion rates and intervals

A thickness number on its own does not say much. What the owner needs is the trend: how fast the wall is thinning at each location, and when it will reach the minimum the design allows. That is why Atlantis records every reading against its grid reference and compares it with the nominal thickness and the previous survey. A drop of a few hundredths of an inch between two annual surveys on a coastal line is a very different message from the same drop on a line that has run for twenty years. Where readings are scattered, repeat scans around the point separate genuine pitting from probe noise.

The owner's inspector uses those figures to set inspection intervals and decide on repair or replacement. We do not set intervals, and we do not declare equipment fit for service. We make sure the data is repeatable, the locations can be found again by the next crew, and any reading near the retirement thickness is flagged in the report summary instead of buried in a table. If the data suggests a change of scope, such as more locations around an elbow that is thinning fast, we say so in the report.

Planning a UT job in Corpus Christi

The Gulf climate sets the practical limits. Humidity and salt air mean surfaces can flash-rust within hours after cleaning, so surface preparation is timed to the examination. Steel surfaces in direct summer sun get far hotter than the air, and standard couplant and probes tolerate only so much, so hot-surface readings use high-temperature probes and couplant and a correction for temperature. Hurricane season from June through November can compress a turnaround or close the port, and outage windows at refineries and terminals are fixed well ahead, so scope and access should be settled before the shutdown begins.

Access matters more than distance. Plants and terminals require site orientation and badging before a technician can work, scaffolding or rope access must be arranged by the owner, and tank and vessel entries need permits. We mobilize technicians from outside the city and travel to your site, so tell us early about badge lead times and any restricted areas. A crew that cannot get through the gate in the first morning is a crew that is not measuring.

UT, MT or PT for your Corpus Christi job

Pick the method by the question. If you need remaining wall or a volumetric view of a weld, ultrasonic testing is the tool. If you are looking for surface cracks in a carbon steel weld, magnetic particle inspection in Corpus Christi is faster and more sensitive at the surface. If the material is stainless, aluminum or a non-magnetic alloy, liquid penetrant testing in Corpus Christi finds what the magnet cannot. Many welds on this coast get a combination, with UT for the volume and MT or PT for the surface. Radiography is not something we perform in the United States, and the radiographic testing page for Corpus Christi explains what we offer instead.

Training your own UT technicians

Many Coastal Bend operators prefer to build their own inspection bench. Our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training cover theory and practice for employers who certify their own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, and the UT simulator lets a candidate rehearse scanning before hands-on time. The employer, not the training provider, certifies the technician. See the Corpus Christi training page for how delivery works.

faq.q: How much of the wall is left, and how does ultrasonic thickness testing show it?
faq.a: A probe sends a sound pulse through the steel and times its return from the back wall. Thickness equals velocity times half that time. Readings are compared with nominal and earlier values to find the corrosion rate at each location.

faq.q: Can UT find cracks that magnetic particle inspection cannot?
faq.a: Yes, for flaws below the surface. Angle-beam UT detects lack of fusion, planar cracks and slag inside a weld, which MT will not show unless they reach or nearly reach the surface. Each method has strengths, so many welds get both.

faq.q: What surface preparation does ultrasonic inspection need in Corpus Christi?
faq.a: The probe has to couple to a reasonably smooth, clean surface. Loose scale, flaking paint and weld spatter are removed, and the area is wiped and examined before humidity and salt air bring back rust. Heavy insulation is stripped locally.

faq.q: Does Atlantis act as the API 510, 570 or 653 inspector?
faq.a: No. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the inspector of record is the one employed or appointed by the owner. Atlantis carries out the ultrasonic examination and reports readings and indications; setting intervals and remaining life stays with that inspector.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a weld in Texas?
faq.a: Sometimes, but only where the construction code allows it and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree before the job. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each have their own provisions, so the contract decides.

faq.q: Can you read hot lines at a refinery or terminal?
faq.a: Hot surfaces can be measured with high-temperature probes and couplant rated for them, and the reading is corrected for temperature. Very hot lines may be scheduled for a shutdown instead, and the technician will say which approach suits the line.

faq.q: What does an ultrasonic report from Atlantis include?
faq.a: It lists the component, procedure and revision, instrument and calibration block, couplant, surface condition, technician and level, and the readings or indications with locations, along with accept or reject against the named code criteria.

faq.q: Do you have an office in Corpus Christi?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Corpus Christi. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so please tell us about badging, permits and access when you ask for a quote.

faq.q: Which codes does ultrasonic work in Corpus Christi usually follow?
faq.a: Typical references are ASME Section V for the method, ASME B31.3 and Section VIII for piping and vessels, API 1104 for pipeline welds and AWS D1.1 or D1.5 for structural and bridge steel. Your contract names the edition.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Corpus Christi, TX
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing of welds, lifting gear and structural steel in Corpus Christi, TX. Ask for an MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Corpus Christi, Texas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection (MPI, also called mag particle testing or MT) in Corpus Christi, Texas. We examine carbon and low-alloy steel welds, lifting equipment, structural connections and fabricated components for surface cracks that other methods miss. Technicians are mobilized to your yard, plant or terminal and follow your procedure or one written to the code. Ask for an MT quote for Corpus Christi; we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing earns its place in Corpus Christi

The Coastal Bend is a place where steel gets welded, loaded, lifted and left outdoors in salt air. Marine and port work puts heavy lifting equipment, padeyes, shackle points and crane structures into service where a hidden fatigue crack can drop a load. Pipe, plate and structural steel pass through the port, so fabrication shops and laydown yards need weld checks before pieces ship. Refineries and terminals along the Inner Harbor have pressure equipment, pipe supports, tank attachments and loading structures that get repaired and re-welded between outages. Wind-energy project cargo and the new Harbor Bridge replacement add large structural welds where fatigue cracks start at the surface.

Magnetic particle inspection suits all of these because the failure to prevent is usually a surface-breaking crack at a weld toe, a fillet, an attachment, or a lifting lug. It also works quickly on field welds in awkward positions, which matters when a tank repair or a vessel nozzle weld has to be signed off before a unit can return to service.

How MT works and which materials it can see

The method magnetizes a ferromagnetic part. A crack or similar discontinuity at the surface disturbs the field and forces some of it to leave the metal, which attracts fine iron particles that are applied to the surface and form a visible line. The result is simple to read and shows the crack length directly.

The same physics sets the limits. MT works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon steel and low-alloy steel, not austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or copper alloys. It finds discontinuities at the surface and slightly below it, but not deep flaws. Sensitivity depends on field direction, since a crack aligned with the field gives a weak indication, which is why the part is examined with the field in two roughly perpendicular directions. Heavy coatings, rust and weld spatter reduce sensitivity and are removed or kept within procedure limits. Where the material is non-magnetic, liquid penetrant testing in Corpus Christi is the usual alternative.

Technique: yokes, prods, wet and dry particles

Most field work in Corpus Christi uses an electromagnetic yoke. ASME Section V Article 7 requires an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke to lift at least 40 pounds, and the yoke is checked against a calibrated weight on a set schedule. Yokes move quickly and leave no arc burns. Prods inject current directly and can be useful on thick sections, but they carry the risk of arc strikes, so many owners prohibit them on pressure boundaries. Coil and central-conductor techniques are used for shop components and shafts.

Particles come in dry powder, wet visible and wet fluorescent forms. Dry visible particles in contrasting colors suit rough field welds outdoors. Wet fluorescent particles give higher sensitivity and are viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area, which is practical in a shop or tent and harder in bright Gulf sunshine. A contrast paint is applied to bare steel where visible particles are used. After the examination, parts that will be welded, machined, coated or placed in service near sensitive equipment are demagnetized, because a residual field can pull arc and swarf and interfere with later steps.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Texas work

The method is written down in ASME Section V Article 7, and ASTM E709 and ASTM E1444 are the guide and practice most often referenced in purchase specifications. Acceptance comes from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 gives MT methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 cover process piping, and AWS D1.1 and D1.5 describe visual and magnetic particle acceptance for structural and bridge steel. For API 510, API 570 and API 653 repairs, the owner's authorized inspector accepts the work; Atlantis reports the indications and does not act as the inspector of record.

In Texas the pressure equipment itself sits under the Texas Boiler Law, administered by the Department of Licensing and Regulation, and repairs and alterations on pressure vessels follow the National Board Inspection Code with an authorized inspector involved. Our Texas inspection page explains the usual sequence from request to report. For method background see magnetic particle testing and the complete guide to magnetic particle testing.

Qualified people and what you receive

Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the technique sheet and reviews the report. Our Level III, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Customers who run their own written practice can have us follow it, and written practice development is available when yours needs work.

The MT report identifies the component and its location, the procedure and revision, the yoke or coil, the lifting-power check, the particle type and color contrast, the light level and the technician with qualification level. Each relevant indication is recorded with position and length, usually with a sketch or photograph, followed by accept or reject against the named criteria and a note on whether demagnetization was performed. We do not report "no indications" without saying what area was cleaned and examined.

Typical components and welds we examine

On port and marine work the list starts with lifting gear: padeyes, lifting lugs, trunnions, spreader beams, shackle bearing areas and the welded attachments on cranes and gantries. Cracks in these start at surface stress concentrations and grow under repeated lifts, so periodic magnetic particle checks are a normal part of a lifting-equipment program. In fabrication shops and yards, MT is applied to fillet welds on structural connections, back-gouged roots, weld repairs after grinding out a defect, and attachment welds on vessel shells such as lugs, clips and supports.

In refinery and terminal work, the same method is used on pipe supports, trunnion welds, nozzle reinforcement pad welds, tank shell-to-bottom attachments and the welds on loading arm structures. Bridge and wind-tower steel adds fatigue-sensitive details such as stiffener ends and flange connections. The procedure names the weld type and the required coverage, and the technician marks the area examined so the extent is clear in the report.

Field details: lighting, contrast and cleaning

Good indications depend on three practical things. Light: visible particles need adequate white light on the surface, and fluorescent particles need UV-A light of the required intensity with low ambient white light. The technician measures both with calibrated meters before the examination and records the readings. Contrast: on bare steel, a thin white contrast paint gives dark particles a clean background, and the paint layer stays thin so it does not mask fine cracks. Cleaning: wire brushing, grinding and solvent wiping remove scale, oil and spatter, but heavy grinding can smear metal over a crack, so cleaning is followed by a close visual check.

The technician also confirms the field strength by watching the pattern on a pie gauge or a shim indicator, a quick way to see that the yoke is producing a usable field in the direction needed. If the yoke cannot be seated on a curved or confined surface, an alternative technique is chosen instead of accepting a weak field. Indications that look like cracks but may be non-relevant, such as those caused by magnetic writing or abrupt changes in section, are re-checked after demagnetization.

Planning an MT job in Corpus Christi

Temperature and moisture are the two things that disturb coastal field MT. Particle suspensions and contrast paints have working ranges, and a steel surface baking in direct summer sun can be too hot for them, while a damp surface after a squall can stop dry powder from moving. Shade, a tent or a different time of day may be needed. Salt air also rusts freshly cleaned steel quickly, so cleaning and examination are paired closely.

Plan around access and permits as much as around the weather. Terminal and refinery work needs site orientation, badging and hot-work or confined-space permits when examining inside a vessel or tank. Port yards have their own security requirements. We travel to your site and mobilize technicians from outside the city, so share gate procedures and outage dates in your request. Black lights and white-light meters are brought and read on site.

Limits to plan around

Magnetic particle inspection is quick, but it is not a universal answer. Thick coatings keep the field from reaching the steel and the particles from reaching a crack, so coating is removed or the procedure is proven with the coating on. Very rough weld caps hold particles and create false patterns. Sections with sharp changes in thickness, such as a nozzle junction, can produce non-relevant indications that look like cracks, and the technician has to separate them from real ones using a second technique or a different field direction. In a tight corner a yoke may not fit, and an alternative technique is needed.

The method also gives no information about depth. A crack that shows at the surface may be shallow or deep, and sizing it for fitness-for-service or repair planning needs another method, usually ultrasonic testing, or careful grinding with repeat checks. We say so in the report and propose the next step instead of leaving the owner to guess.

Choosing between MT, UT and PT in Corpus Christi

If the suspect flaw is a surface crack in carbon steel, MT is usually the fastest and most sensitive field test. If you need remaining wall or want to see inside a weld, ultrasonic testing in Corpus Christi adds the volume view. If the metal is stainless or non-ferrous, use penetrant. Some welds need two methods because each sees something the other cannot. Radiographic testing is not offered by Atlantis in the United States; read the radiographic testing page for Corpus Christi for what we can do. See also MT versus PT compared when you are weighing the two surface methods.

Training your own MT technicians

Operators who want an in-house surface inspection capability can start with MT Level 1 training and move on to MT Level 2 training, with magnetic particle testing training describing the syllabus. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so the course supports your program rather than replacing it. The Corpus Christi training page covers how sessions work and the eligibility checker shows the hours and vision requirements.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be done on stainless steel in Corpus Christi?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel is not ferromagnetic, so MT does not work on it. Aluminum and copper alloys are in the same position. Liquid penetrant testing is the normal surface method for those materials.

faq.q: What indications does MT find in a weld?
faq.a: MT detects surface cracks, lack of fusion open to the surface, laps and seams, and some near-surface flaws. Deep subsurface discontinuities are better found with ultrasonic testing, and the right method depends on the code.

faq.q: Do I need to clean welds before magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Yes. Loose scale, oil, grease, weld spatter and heavy paint are removed so particles can reach the surface and move freely. Thin, tight coatings are acceptable only if the procedure has been demonstrated with them.

faq.q: Why are two field directions needed?
faq.a: A crack is easiest to see when it lies across the magnetic field. By magnetizing in two roughly perpendicular directions, the examination catches cracks regardless of their orientation, as ASME Section V Article 7 requires.

faq.q: Is wet fluorescent MT practical outdoors on the coast?
faq.a: It needs a darkened area for UV-A viewing, so tents or covers are used outdoors. Visible dry or wet particles with contrast paint are often chosen for open field welds in bright sunshine.

faq.q: When is demagnetization required after MT?
faq.a: When a residual field would interfere with later welding, machining, coating or service, the part is demagnetized and checked. The procedure and customer specification say when that is needed, and the report records it.

faq.q: Will Atlantis perform the MT work as the API 653 inspector?
faq.a: No. Atlantis reports what the magnetic particle examination shows; accepting or rejecting a repair under API 653 is decided by the owner's authorized inspector, who is the inspector of record.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Corpus Christi office?
faq.a: No. We have no office in the city. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, so please give us badge, permit and access details when you request the work.

faq.q: Which code sets MT acceptance for my vessel or piping?
faq.a: The construction code does. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 and AWS D1.1 each give their own criteria, and your contract names the edition we apply.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant, Corpus Christi TX
pt.description: Dye penetrant inspection (PT) of stainless, aluminum and carbon steel welds in Corpus Christi, TX plants, terminals and yards. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Corpus Christi, Texas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection or PT, in Corpus Christi, Texas. It is the surface method for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and any other non-porous metal that magnetic particle inspection cannot test, and it works equally well on carbon steel. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, terminal or yard to examine welds, castings and repairs for cracks that break the surface. Request a PT quote for Corpus Christi and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant inspection is used around Corpus Christi

Corpus Christi processes and ships energy and bulk materials through the port, and much of the equipment involved is not carbon steel. Refinery and petrochemical units use austenitic stainless steel and duplex alloys in heat exchanger tubing and shells, reactor internals, furnace outlet piping and corrosion-resistant overlays. LNG liquefaction and export facilities on the La Quinta side rely on stainless and nickel-alloy piping for cold service. Marine vessels calling at the port have aluminum structure, stainless piping and non-magnetic fittings. Fabrication yards add stainless pipe spools, aluminum lifting beams and weld repairs on cast components.

For all of those, penetrant testing is the method that works. It also serves carbon steel jobs where magnetic particle testing is impractical, such as small bores, tight geometries or places where the magnetizing equipment cannot be placed, and it is commonly specified for final inspection of weld overlay and for tubing and nozzle welds.

What PT finds, and the one thing it cannot do

Penetrant inspection detects only discontinuities that are open to the surface. The liquid enters the crack by capillary action, the excess is removed, and a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so the crack appears as a bright line or spot. That makes PT very sensitive to fine cracks, porosity at the surface, laps and shrinkage cracks, and the shape and length are easy to measure on the part.

It cannot see a flaw that does not reach the surface. A crack closed by peening, grinding smear, shot blasting or a heavy coating will not accept penetrant, and so surface preparation is part of the test, not an optional extra. Porous materials, rough surfaces that trap penetrant and surfaces contaminated with oil or paint give false or masked results. For a flaw below the surface, ultrasonic testing is the tool, and our ultrasonic testing page for Corpus Christi describes it. For carbon steel where a magnet is practical, see magnetic particle inspection in Corpus Christi.

Technique: penetrant types, removal and developer

Penetrants are classed as visible (usually red) or fluorescent, and as water washable, post-emulsifiable or solvent removable. On Corpus Christi field work, solvent-removable visible penetrant is the usual choice for welds and repairs because it is portable and does not need water or a darkened area. Fluorescent penetrant, viewed under UV-A light, is more sensitive and used in shops and for critical parts. Sulfur and chlorine contamination matters on stainless steel and nickel alloys, so penetrant materials for those jobs are certified low in halogens and sulfur by the supplier lot.

The sequence is fixed: clean and dry the surface, apply penetrant and hold for the dwell time in the procedure, remove the excess carefully so the penetrant is not washed out of the crack, apply a thin even coat of developer, and examine during the development time. Over-cleaning with solvent or over-wiping can remove penetrant from a real crack, and a thick developer coat can hide fine indications, so the technician controls each step. Afterwards, the part is cleaned to remove residue when the procedure requires it.

Temperature limits and the Gulf Coast climate

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the standard temperature range for the part and the penetrant materials at between 40 and 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside that range, the procedure must be qualified at the temperature in use. In Corpus Christi this is a real constraint, not a footnote. Steel exposed to direct summer sun routinely exceeds 125 degrees even when the air is cooler, which causes penetrant to dry on the surface and developer to bake. Shading the part and letting it cool, or using a qualified high-temperature procedure, are the practical answers.

Cold is occasional rather than routine on this coast, but a winter front can push a surface below 40 degrees and slow penetrant action, and humid mornings cause condensation on cold steel. The technician measures surface temperature before starting and records it in the report. Wind-blown sand and spray near the port can contaminate the developer coat, so wind screens and fresh materials are brought for outdoor work.

Codes, acceptance and the Texas context

The method itself is written in ASME Section V Article 6, with ASTM E165 and E1417 commonly referenced in customer specifications. Acceptance criteria come from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 covers penetrant methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 covers process piping. Rounded and linear indications are judged separately, with limits on size and spacing. Where AWS D1.6 or customer specifications govern stainless fabrication, we work to the stated criteria.

For repairs on boilers and pressure vessels in Texas, the National Board Inspection Code applies and an authorized inspector accepts the work under the Texas Boiler Law administered by the Department of Licensing and Regulation. Under API 510, 570 and 653, the owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record, while Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and reports the findings. The Texas inspection hub and the national penetrant testing page give more background, and the Article 6 explainer walks through the procedure requirements.

Weld overlay, tubing and repair welds

Three kinds of work account for most penetrant jobs on this coast. The first is stainless and alloy weld overlay and cladding inside vessels and on heat exchanger tubesheets, where a crack that reaches the surface can open a path for corrosion to the base metal. The second is pipe and nozzle welds in stainless or duplex materials, including root passes examined before the weld is completed and final caps afterwards. The third is repair welds: when a defect is ground out of a carbon or alloy part, penetrant checks the excavation to confirm the crack has been removed before welding resumes, and again after the repair weld is finished.

In each case the technician decides how much surface to clean around the weld and records the area examined. Overlay examinations need bright metal with no trapped moisture or grinding smear. Root-pass checks need a dry joint and attention to residue, because penetrant left in a crevice can contaminate the next weld pass. We handle this with the cleaning steps in the procedure and by timing the examination to the welding sequence.

People, procedures and the report

Our PT technicians are qualified under the company written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II personnel apply the process and interpret indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The company's founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT and approves our penetrant procedures. When a customer provides its own procedure, we follow it; when it needs one, our Level III writes it to the code edition named in the contract.

The report names the component and location, the procedure and revision, the penetrant, remover and developer by manufacturer and lot, the surface temperature, dwell and development times, the technician and level, and any indications with size, location and a photograph or sketch. Each result closes with an accept or reject call against the criteria in your contract. A statement that no indications were found includes the area covered and the condition of the surface at the time.

Planning a PT job in Corpus Christi

Start with surface condition. Stainless piping in a refinery often arrives with a layer of paint, insulation residue or salt, and weld overlay on a heat exchanger needs clean, bright metal before penetrant is applied. Allow time for cleaning and drying, because trapped solvent can ruin a test. Coordinate with the owner on what chemicals are allowed near sensitive equipment and in confined spaces, and make sure ventilation and hot-work rules are covered in the permit.

Site entry is the other planning item. Plants and terminals usually require orientation, badging and in some cases escorts. We travel to your site and mobilize technicians from outside the city, so tell us about gate procedures, laydown space and where materials may be stored. If the work will be outdoors, ask for shade or a temporary shelter, which saves time and keeps you within the procedure temperature range.

What a good penetrant result looks like

A clean penetrant examination does not mean a quick one. After development, the surface should show an even, thin coat of developer and a clear background with no heavy pink bleed. A crack appears as a continuous or broken line that bleeds out slowly over the development time, and rounded porosity appears as isolated dots. The technician examines the surface while it develops, not only at the end, because a fine crack can spread into a blur if left too long. Doubtful indications are wiped away and the area is retested after fresh cleaning, which confirms whether the indication reappears.

Photographs with a scale help the owner see what was found. Indications are described by type, length and location, and the report says whether each was accepted or rejected against the named criteria. If the surface condition prevented a reliable test, such as a rough weld cap or porous casting, the report records the limitation and the follow-up suggested.

PT, MT or UT for your Corpus Christi component

A simple rule works: if the material is non-magnetic, use penetrant for surface cracks; if it is carbon steel, magnetic particle testing is usually quicker; if you need the volume of a weld, add ultrasonic testing. Many stainless welds get penetrant on the root and cap and ultrasonic testing for the body. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and the radiographic testing page for Corpus Christi explains how we can help when your specification calls for it. Our MT versus PT comparison sets out the differences in detail.

Training penetrant technicians

If you want to qualify your own staff, PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training cover the theory and practical skills, penetrant testing training gives the outline, and the penetrant testing simulator offers practice before live specimens. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. See the Corpus Christi training page for delivery details.

faq.q: What is the difference between dye penetrant inspection and liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: They are the same method. Liquid penetrant testing is the formal name, and dye penetrant inspection describes the visible-dye version. Fluorescent penetrant is the other main type and is viewed under ultraviolet light.

faq.q: Can PT find cracks below the surface of a weld?
faq.a: No. Penetrant detects only flaws that are open to the surface, because the liquid has to enter the crack. Subsurface flaws need ultrasonic testing, and near-surface flaws in carbon steel may be found by magnetic particle testing.

faq.q: What temperature range does penetrant testing allow?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 sets the standard range at 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the materials. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified, which matters on sun-heated steel in Corpus Christi.

faq.q: Why does stainless steel need low-halogen penetrant materials?
faq.a: Chlorine and sulfur left on stainless steel or nickel alloys can cause cracking or corrosion in service. Penetrant materials for those jobs are supplied with low-halogen and low-sulfur lot certification, and the lots are recorded in the report.

faq.q: How long does the penetrant need to sit on the surface?
faq.a: The procedure sets the dwell time for the penetrant, the material and the temperature. The technician follows that time and the developer time exactly, because too little or too much can hide a real crack.

faq.q: Can PT be used on aluminum and other non-magnetic metals?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant works on aluminum, stainless, copper alloys and many other non-porous metals, which is why it is the surface method of choice when magnetic particle inspection is not possible.

faq.q: Does Atlantis serve as the API 510 or 570 inspector for PT work?
faq.a: No. Under API 510 and 570 the owner's own authorized inspector signs as inspector of record. Atlantis does the penetrant examination and passes the findings along for that inspector to review.

faq.q: Does Atlantis maintain a Corpus Christi office?
faq.a: No. We have no office there. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, so please tell us about badging, permits and access when you ask for a quote.

faq.q: What surface preparation does PT need before examination?
faq.a: The surface must be clean and dry, free of oil, paint, scale, weld spatter and chemical residue. Grinding, peening or blasting that smears metal over a crack can hide it and may call for etching or re-cleaning.

rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. See UT as a volumetric alternative and Level III review of radiographs for Corpus Christi, TX work.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Corpus Christi, Texas: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
In the United States, Atlantis does not perform radiography of any kind, and that includes Corpus Christi. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission sets the rules in 10 CFR Part 34, and Agreement States such as Texas administer equivalent requirements for their own licensees. It is not a service Atlantis offers in Corpus Christi or anywhere else in the country. If your specification calls for radiography on refinery, terminal, pipeline or fabrication welds, you will need a licensed radiography contractor, and we do not recommend one. What we can do is help with the surrounding decisions, described below.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

Some codes and owners accept ultrasonic examination in place of radiography on production welds. ASME B31.3 contains provisions for ultrasonic examination of welds, API 1104 allows it for pipeline girth welds, and AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds in structural steel. ASME Section VIII lets ultrasonic testing replace radiography only under specific conditions, so the substitution is never assumed. The owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector have to agree before the job begins, and the written procedure must reflect that agreement.

Where substitution is allowed, angle-beam shear-wave examination gives a volumetric view of the weld and can find lack of fusion and cracks that film often misses at unfavorable angles. It also needs no exclusion zone and no radiation controls, which is a practical advantage on a busy Corpus Christi turnaround. See ultrasonic testing in Corpus Christi for how we perform it.

ASNT Level III review of radiographs and procedures

Reviewing a radiograph does not require a radiation licence, because the reviewer handles images, not sources. Our ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, give a second read on disputed or borderline indications, and check a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice for gaps. Our reviewer would be Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

This can be useful to owners who receive a package of film from a contractor and want an independent view before accepting a repair, or to fabricators who need a second opinion on a rejected weld. It is a document and image review. We do not take the exposure, and we do not sign for a contractor's work. For wider help see Level III consulting and written practice development.

Surface methods that still apply

Many weld problems in Corpus Christi are surface-breaking, and two methods we do perform cover them. Magnetic particle inspection in Corpus Christi finds cracks at the surface of carbon and low-alloy steel, and liquid penetrant testing in Corpus Christi does the same on stainless steel, aluminum and other non-magnetic metals. They do not replace radiography where the code requires a volumetric method, but they reduce the number of welds that fail at the surface before a licensed contractor is called in.

Radiography theory and training

If you want your own people to understand radiography, our RT Level 2 course covers the theory and film interpretation that SNT-TC-1A-based programs expect. The employer certifies under its own written practice, and handling radioactive sources or x-ray equipment still requires the licences and radiation safety training that regulators set. Our Corpus Christi training page explains how training is delivered.

How to ask for help

Tell us the code, the weld type, the thickness range and what your specification actually requires. If it names radiography without an alternative, you will need a licensed contractor, and we can still review their output. If the code permits ultrasonic examination, we can propose a procedure for your owner's approval. Ask about RT alternatives for Corpus Christi; we reply within one business day. Technicians who perform ultrasonic work are mobilized to your site, and the Texas inspection page gives more context.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Corpus Christi?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography anywhere in the United States, because it is a licensed activity under NRC rules or Agreement State equivalents. We offer ultrasonic testing, magnetic particle, penetrant and Level III review instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be used in place of radiography on my weld?
faq.a: Possibly, if the construction code allows it and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree before the job. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each have provisions, but Section VIII allows it only under specific conditions.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs from another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the code, and can give a second read on disputed indications. This is a review, not a new exposure.

faq.q: Can you recommend a radiography contractor in Corpus Christi?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. Your owner or the Texas regulator can confirm a contractor holds the required licence. We can review their procedure and written practice if you ask.

faq.q: Do you teach radiography?
faq.a: The RT Level 2 course teaches the theory that employers expect from candidates they certify under their own SNT-TC-1A program. Handling sources or x-ray equipment still requires regulatory licences and radiation safety training set by the state.
